claim: Epidermal cells show smaller and larger vacuolar structures in shorter tricho- and longer atrichoblast cells, respectively.
source: Epidermal cells show smaller and larger vacuolar structures in shorter tricho- and longer atrichoblast cells, respectively (Berger et al., 1998; Löfke et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Berger et al., 1998; Löfke et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1A showing the differential vacuolar structures.

claim: Exogenous application of auxin (NAA [250 nM]) leads to a dramatic change in vacuolar appearance in root epidermal cells, which display smaller luminal vacuolar structures.
source: Remarkably, exogenous application of auxin (NAA [250 nM]) or endogenous elevation of YUCCA-dependent auxin biosynthesis led to a dramatic change in vacuolar appearance in root epidermal cells, which consequently displayed smaller luminal vacuolar structures (Figure 1A,B,E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,E,F demonstrating auxin-induced changes in vacuolar morphology.

claim: Endogenous elevation of YUCCA-dependent auxin biosynthesis leads to a dramatic change in vacuolar appearance in root epidermal cells, which display smaller luminal vacuolar structures.
source: Remarkably, exogenous application of auxin (NAA [250 nM]) or endogenous elevation of YUCCA-dependent auxin biosynthesis led to a dramatic change in vacuolar appearance in root epidermal cells, which consequently displayed smaller luminal vacuolar structures (Figure 1A,B,E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,E,F demonstrating genetic manipulation of auxin levels affects vacuolar morphology.

claim: High auxin conditions affect vacuolar structures, particularly in atrichoblasts.
source: This analysis revealed that high auxin conditions affect vacuolar structures, particularly in atrichoblasts (Figure 1D,G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D,G demonstrating differential effects on atrichoblasts.

claim: Pharmacological depletion of auxin causes visibly larger vacuolar structures in both cell types, but is more pronounced in trichoblasts (relative to the untreated control).
source: Adversely, pharmacological depletion of auxin caused visibly larger vacuolar structures in both cell types, but was more pronounced in trichoblasts (relative to the untreated control) (Figure 1A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C,D demonstrating effects of auxin biosynthesis inhibitor kynurenin.

claim: High auxin levels reduce the cell length of atrichoblast cells.
source: High auxin levels reduced the cell length of atrichoblast cells (Figure 1A,B,E,F,H,I), whereas cell lengths of the smaller trichoblasts were not significantly affected (Figure 1A,B,E,F,H,I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1H,I demonstrating cell length changes under high auxin conditions.

claim: Cell lengths of the smaller trichoblasts are not significantly affected by high auxin levels.
source: High auxin levels reduced the cell length of atrichoblast cells (Figure 1A,B,E,F,H,I), whereas cell lengths of the smaller trichoblasts were not significantly affected (Figure 1A,B,E,F,H,I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1H,I demonstrating differential effects on trichoblasts versus atrichoblasts.

claim: Pharmacological reduction in auxin biosynthesis mainly increases the cell length in trichoblasts.
source: Conversely, pharmacological reduction in auxin biosynthesis mainly increased the cell length in trichoblasts (Figure 1A,C,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C,H demonstrating effects of kynurenin treatment on cell length.

claim: Auxin treatments do not reverse vacuolar morphology of fully elongated epidermal root cells in the differentiation zone.
source: Auxin treatments manifestly did not reverse vacuolar morphology of fully elongated epidermal root cells in the differentiation zone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrating lack of effect in differentiated cells.

claim: Auxin mainly shapes vacuoles in growth competent cells.
source: This finding suggests that auxin mainly shapes vacuoles in growth competent cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that auxin affects vacuoles in late meristematic cells but not in fully elongated cells in the differentiation zone.

claim: Auxin induces detectable changes in vacuolar morphology after 15–30 min.
source: Auxin induced detectable changes in vacuolar morphology already after 15–30 min (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by time course experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The auxin effect on late meristematic cell size starts to be significantly affected around 45 min.
source: On the other hand the auxin effect on late meristematic cell size was slightly later starting to be significantly affected around 45 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by time course experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The auxin effect on vacuolar morphology precedes the auxin impact on late meristematic cell size.
source: Based on our time course experiments we conclude that the auxin effect on vacuolar morphology precedes the auxin impact on late meristematic cell size.
evidence: Supported by time course data showing vacuolar changes at 15-30 min and cell size changes at 45 min.

claim: Auxin analogue 5-F-IAA preferentially triggers genomic auxin responses via TIR1/AFBs.
source: It has been suggested that auxin analogue 5-F-IAA preferentially triggers genomic auxin responses via TIR1/AFBs (Robert et al., 2010) and it indeed induced small luminal vacuoles (Figure 3A,B,E).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robert et al., 2010 and experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B,E.

claim: 5-F-IAA induces small luminal vacuoles.
source: It has been suggested that auxin analogue 5-F-IAA preferentially triggers genomic auxin responses via TIR1/AFBs (Robert et al., 2010) and it indeed induced small luminal vacuoles (Figure 3A,B,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B,E.

claim: Auxinole, a designated inhibitor of TIR1/AFBs auxin receptors, blocks the auxin effect on vacuolar morphology.
source: Correspondingly, auxinole, a designated inhibitor of TIR1/AFBs auxin receptors (Hayashi et al., 2012), blocked the auxin effect on vacuolar morphology (Figure 3A,C,D,E), and, the genetic reduction of TIR1/AFBs functions in tir1 afb1 afb3 triple mutants prompted partial resistance to the auxin-induced changes in vacuolar appearance (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,C,D,E demonstrating pharmacological inhibition of TIR1/AFBs.

claim: The genetic reduction of TIR1/AFBs functions in tir1 afb1 afb3 triple mutants prompts partial resistance to the auxin-induced changes in vacuolar appearance.
source: Correspondingly, auxinole, a designated inhibitor of TIR1/AFBs auxin receptors (Hayashi et al., 2012), blocked the auxin effect on vacuolar morphology (Figure 3A,C,D,E), and, the genetic reduction of TIR1/AFBs functions in tir1 afb1 afb3 triple mutants prompted partial resistance to the auxin-induced changes in vacuolar appearance (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–J demonstrating genetic reduction of TIR1/AFBs function.

claim: TIR1/AFBs-dependent auxin signalling is required for the auxin effect on vacuolar morphogenesis.
source: This set of data indicates that TIR1/AFBs-dependent auxin signalling is required for the auxin effect on vacuolar morphogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological and genetic experiments showing that interference with TIR1/AFBs blocks auxin effects on vacuoles.

claim: Increased auxin biosynthesis or exogenous application of auxin increases the fluorescence intensity of tonoplast localised SNAREs, such as VAMP711-YFP, SYP21-YFP and SYP22-GFP.
source: Remarkably, increased auxin biosynthesis or exogenous application of auxin increased the fluorescence intensity of tonoplast localised SNAREs, such as VAMP711-YFP, SYP21-YFP and SYP22-GFP (Figure 4A–L,N,O).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–L,N,O demonstrating increased SNARE fluorescence under high auxin conditions.

claim: The auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs does not rely on membrane crowding.
source: Notably, VAMP711-RFP/YFP, but not the membrane dyes showed auxin-induced signal intensities, suggesting that the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs does not rely on membrane crowding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by co-localization experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 comparing VAMP711 with membrane dyes.

claim: The auxin effect on SNAREs does not indirectly rely on cytosolic pH.
source: The auxin effect on VAMP711 was detectable in both pH sensitive YFP and pH resistant RFP fusions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B; Figure 5A,B), suggesting that the auxin effect on SNAREs does not indirectly rely on cytosolic pH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing auxin effects on both YFP and RFP fusions, ruling out pH sensitivity as a confounding factor.

claim: Auxin increases cellular SNARE abundance at the tonoplast.
source: Subsequent maximum projections and intensity measurements confirmed that auxin increases cellular SNARE abundance at the tonoplast (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–I).
evidence: Supported by z-stack imaging and maximum projection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–I.

claim: Auxin increases vacuolar SNARE abundance as confirmed by western blots on excised root tips.
source: To further emphasize on this finding, we also performed western blots on excised root tips, similarly confirming our conclusion that auxin increases vacuolar SNARE abundance (Figure 4M,P).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4M,P.

claim: Tonoplast marker NET4A-GFP does not show auxin-induced stabilization.
source: Notably, tonoplast marker NET4A-GFP (Deeks et al., 2012) did not show auxin-induced stabilization (Figure 4G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2G,H), suggesting certain specificity for the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G,H demonstrating lack of auxin effect on NET4A-GFP.

claim: Induction of a single SNARE component, such as VAMP711, does not affect vacuolar morphogenesis.
source: Induction of a single SNARE component, such as VAMP711, did not affect vacuolar morphogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), possibly indicating the joint requirement of several complex components.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Auxin modulates SNARE proteins when expressed under constitutive promoters.
source: Furthermore, auxin modulated SNARE proteins also when expressed under constitutive promoters (Figure 4A–D,I–N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–D,I–N.

claim: Auxin affects the vacuolar SNAREs posttranslationally.
source: This data implies that auxin affects the vacuolar SNAREs posttranslationally.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that auxin modulates SNAREs expressed under constitutive promoters, indicating post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: Concomitant treatments with auxin and the TIR1/AFBs antagonist auxinole comprehensively interfere with auxin-induced stabilisation of VAMP711-YFP.
source: Concomitant treatments with auxin and the TIR1/AFBs antagonist auxinole comprehensively interfered with auxin-induced stabilisation of VAMP711-YFP (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–E demonstrating pharmacological inhibition of auxin effect on VAMP711.

claim: The auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs is significantly reduced in the tir1 afb1 afb3 triple mutant.
source: Concurrently, the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs was also significantly reduced in the tir1 afb1 afb3 triple mutant (Figure 5F–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–J demonstrating genetic reduction of TIR1/AFBs function.

claim: TIR1/AFBs-dependent auxin signalling triggers higher SNARE abundance at the tonoplast.
source: We conclude that the TIR1/AFBs-dependent auxin signalling triggers higher SNARE abundance at the tonoplast.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological and genetic experiments showing that TIR1/AFBs are required for auxin-induced SNARE stabilization.

claim: Most analysed SNARE single mutants display vacuolar morphology reminiscent to wild type.
source: It has been suggested that several vacuolar SNARE components act redundantly (Yano et al., 2003; Uemura et al., 2010) and also in our conditions most analysed SNARE single mutants displayed vacuolar morphology reminiscent to wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: vti11 mutant alleles display roundish vacuoles in untreated conditions.
source: In contrast, vti11 mutant alleles display roundish vacuoles in untreated conditions (Yano et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2014) (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,C and citations to previous work.

claim: Vacuoles remain differentially controlled in vti11 mutant tricho- and atrichoblast cells.
source: Despite these apparent defects, vacuoles remained differentially controlled in vti11 mutant tricho- and atrichoblast cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that the cell type-dependent regulation of vacuolar morphology is at least partially operational in vti11 mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Auxin treatments are less effective to modulate vacuolar morphology in vti11 mutants.
source: Auxin treatments were less effective to modulate vacuolar morphology in vti11 mutants (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–E demonstrating reduced auxin sensitivity in vti11 mutants.

claim: pVTI11:VTI11-GFP expression in vti11 mutant cells induces reversion to auxin sensitive vacuolar morphology.
source: Notably, pVTI11:VTI11-GFP expression in vti11 mutant cells induced reversion to auxin sensitive vacuolar morphology (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by complementation experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Auxin does not only affect SNARE abundance, but requires functional Q-SNARE VTI11 to modulate vacuolar shapes.
source: This data indicates that auxin does not only affect SNARE abundance, but requires functional Q-SNARE VTI11 to modulate vacuolar shapes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that vti11 mutants show reduced auxin sensitivity and complementation restores auxin sensitivity.

claim: vti11 mutants are less sensitive to the negative impact of auxin on late meristematic cell size.
source: Interestingly, vti11 mutants were not only partially resistant to the auxin effect on vacuoles, but in addition, less sensitive to the negative impact of auxin on late meristematic cell size (Figure 6A–D,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–D,F demonstrating reduced auxin sensitivity in cell size regulation.

claim: VTI11 function is required for the auxin effect on vacuolar shape and late meristematic cell size.
source: This data suggests that VTI11 function is required for the auxin effect on vacuolar shape and late meristematic cell size.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that vti11 mutants show reduced auxin sensitivity in both vacuolar morphology and cell size.

claim: PI3/4 kinase inhibitor Wortmannin (WM) affects vacuolar morphology.
source: PI3/4 kinase inhibitor Wortmannin (WM) affects vacuolar morphology and has been recently proffered as affecting processes upstream of vacuolar SNAREs in plants (Feraru et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Feraru et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2014).

claim: WM treatments lead to larger luminal vacuoles and abolish the auxin effect on vacuoles.
source: WM treatments led to larger luminal vacuoles and abolished the auxin effect on vacuoles (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–E demonstrating WM effects on vacuolar morphology.

claim: The negative effect of auxin on limiting late meristematic cell size is abolished after low doses of WM [2 µM].
source: It may be noted that the negative effect of auxin on limiting late meristematic cell size was also abolished after low doses of WM [2 µM] (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F demonstrating WM effects on cell size regulation.

claim: WM sensitive processes may contribute to auxin-dependent vacuolar morphogenesis and cell size regulation.
source: This data suggests that WM sensitive processes may contribute to auxin-dependent vacuolar morphogenesis and cell size regulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that WM abolishes auxin effects on both vacuolar morphology and cell size.

claim: pi4kß1/2 double mutants show partially auxin resistant vacuolar appearance compared to wild-type seedlings.
source: Compared to wild-type seedlings, pi4kß1/2 double mutants showed partially auxin resistant vacuolar appearance (Figure 7H–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H–L demonstrating genetic reduction of PI4Kß function.

claim: The genetic interference with PI4Kß-function abolishes the auxin effect on reducing late meristematic cell size.
source: Moreover, the genetic interference with PI4Kß-function was reminiscent of WM treatments and also abolished the auxin effect on reducing late meristematic cell size (Figure 7M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7M demonstrating effects of pi4kß1/2 mutation on cell size regulation.

claim: PI-dependent processes affect auxin-dependent vacuolar morphology.
source: Based on our pharmacological and genetic data, we conclude that PI-dependent processes affect auxin-dependent vacuolar morphology.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological (WM) and genetic (pi4kß1/2) experiments showing effects on auxin-dependent vacuolar morphology.

claim: Concomitant treatments with PI3/4-kinase inhibitor WM and auxin completely diminish the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs even at relatively high auxin levels (NAA [500 nM]).
source: Concomitant treatments with PI3/4-kinase inhibitor WM and auxin completely diminished the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs even at relatively high auxin levels (NAA [500 nM]) (Figure 7G; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: WM sensitive processes interfere with both the auxin effect on vacuolar morphology and the auxin-dependent regulation of vacuolar SNARE abundance.
source: This data suggests that WM sensitive processes interfere with both the auxin effect on vacuolar morphology and the auxin-dependent regulation of vacuolar SNARE abundance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that WM blocks both auxin effects on vacuolar morphology and SNARE abundance.

claim: The pi4kß1/2 double mutants show reduced VAMP711-YFP abundance in untreated and auxin treated conditions.
source: Analogously, the pi4kß1/2 double mutants showed reduced VAMP711-YFP abundance in untreated and auxin treated conditions (Figure 7N; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7N and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Auxin requires PI4K activity to modulate vacuolar SNAREs.
source: We accordingly conclude that auxin requires PI4K activity to modulate vacuolar SNAREs.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological and genetic experiments showing that PI4K activity is required for auxin effects on SNAREs.

claim: SNARE stability is still increased in response to high auxin (NAA [500 nM]) in pi4kß1/2 double mutants.
source: In contrast to WM, SNARE stability was still increased in response to high auxin (NAA [500 nM]) in pi4kß1/2 double mutants (Figure 7N; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7N and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: pi4kß1/2 double mutants show auxin sensitive vacuolar morphogenesis at higher auxin levels.
source: Notably, pi4kß1/2 double mutants showed auxin sensitive vacuolar morphogenesis at these higher auxin levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: PI4 kinase activity and possibly other, WM sensitive, PI-dependent processes affect auxin-dependent posttranslational regulation of vacuolar SNARE proteins.
source: Based on this data, we assume that PI4 kinase activity and possibly other, WM sensitive, PI-dependent processes affect auxin-dependent posttranslational regulation of vacuolar SNARE proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of WM and pi4kß1/2 mutation on auxin-dependent SNARE regulation.

claim: The PI-dependent interference with the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs completely coincides with a reduced impact of auxin on vacuolar morphology and meristematic cell size.
source: We conclude that the PI-dependent interference with the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs completely coincides with a reduced impact of auxin on vacuolar morphology and meristematic cell size.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between PI-dependent effects on SNAREs, vacuolar morphology, and cell size.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of PI3 and PI4 kinases leads to reduced sensitivity to auxin-dependent inhibition of epidermal growth.
source: As expected, auxin repressed cellular elongation in wild-type epidermal cells (Figure 8A,B). In contrast, pharmacological inhibition of PI3 and PI4 kinases led to reduced sensitivity to auxin-dependent inhibition of epidermal growth (Figure 8C,D,I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C,D,I demonstrating WM effects on cellular elongation.

claim: pi4kß1/2 double mutants are resistant to the auxin-dependent inhibition of cellular expansion.
source: pi4kß1/2 double mutants were similarly resistant to the auxin-dependent inhibition of cellular expansion (Figure 8E,F,J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E,F,J demonstrating genetic effects on cellular expansion.

claim: Exogenous application of auxin strongly reduces the root length of wild-type seedlings.
source: Exogenous application of auxin strongly reduced the root length of wild-type seedlings, but was less effective following pharmacological (WM treated wild-type) and genetic interference (pi4kß1/2 double) with PI kinases (Figure 8L–N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8L–N demonstrating auxin effects on root growth.

claim: Auxin is less effective at reducing root length following pharmacological (WM treated wild-type) and genetic interference (pi4kß1/2 double) with PI kinases.
source: Exogenous application of auxin strongly reduced the root length of wild-type seedlings, but was less effective following pharmacological (WM treated wild-type) and genetic interference (pi4kß1/2 double) with PI kinases (Figure 8L–N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8L–N demonstrating reduced auxin sensitivity in WM-treated and pi4kß1/2 mutant plants.

claim: Increased auxin concentrations lead to root growth inhibition also in pi4kß1/2 double mutants.
source: Notably and comparable with our cellular analysis, increased auxin concentrations led to root growth inhibition also in pi4kß1/2 double mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: PI-dependent processes contribute to auxin-dependent inhibition of cellular and root organ growth.
source: In conclusion, this data suggests that PI-dependent processes contribute to auxin-dependent inhibition of cellular and root organ growth.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological and genetic experiments showing that PI-dependent processes are required for auxin effects on growth.

claim: Cellular elongation is less sensitive to auxin in vti11 mutants.
source: In agreement with our data on meristematic cell size control, cellular elongation was also less sensitive to auxin in vit11 mutants (Figure 8G,H,K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8G,H,K demonstrating reduced auxin sensitivity in vti11 mutants.

claim: The negative effect of auxin on root organ growth is reduced in vti11 mutants.
source: The negative effect of auxin on root organ growth was also reduced in vti11 mutants (Figure 8L,O), but was complemented by VTI11-GFP expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8L,O and complementation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Auxin requires VTI11 function to inhibit cellular expansion and root organ growth.
source: Therefore, we conclude that auxin requires VTI11 function to inhibit cellular expansion and moreover root organ growth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that vti11 mutants show reduced auxin sensitivity in both cellular expansion and root growth.

claim: Auxin interferes with SNARE abundance at the tonoplast, correlating with its effect on vacuolar morphology.
source: We have demonstrated that auxin interferes with SNARE abundance at the tonoplast, correlating with its effect on vacuolar morphology.
evidence: Summarizes experimental findings showing correlation between auxin effects on SNAREs and vacuolar morphology.

claim: Auxin-dependent modulation of vacuolar shape precisely coincides with auxin dependent growth inhibition.
source: What is striking is that auxin-dependent modulation of vacuolar shape precisely coincides with auxin dependent growth inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal and functional correlation between auxin effects on vacuolar morphology and growth inhibition.

claim: Pharmacological and genetic interference with the auxin-dependent regulation of SNARE abundance corresponds with auxin resistant vacuolar morphology.
source: Pharmacological and genetic interference with the auxin-dependent regulation of SNARE abundance corresponds with auxin resistant vacuolar morphology.
evidence: Summarizes experimental findings showing that interference with SNARE regulation leads to auxin-resistant vacuolar morphology.

claim: Abrogation of the cellular auxin effect on vacuolar morphology interrelates with lower sensitivity to auxin-dependent inhibition of cellular growth.
source: Moreover, abrogation of the cellular auxin effect on vacuolar morphology interrelates with lower sensitivity to auxin-dependent inhibition of cellular growth.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between auxin-resistant vacuolar morphology and reduced auxin sensitivity in growth inhibition.

claim: Auxin signalling utilises SNARE-dependent vacuolar morphogenesis to restrict cellular expansion.
source: We propose, based on these independent lines of evidence, that auxin signalling utilises SNARE-dependent vacuolar morphogenesis to restrict cellular expansion.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on multiple lines of experimental evidence showing correlation between auxin effects on SNAREs, vacuolar morphology, and growth.

claim: SNARE-dependent vacuolar morphogenesis regulation could have widespread developmental consequences, such as determining root organ growth rates.
source: Such regulation could have widespread developmental consequences, such as determining root organ growth rates.
evidence: Speculative statement about broader implications of the findings.

claim: The morphology of plant vacuoles correlates with cell size.
source: It has been noted that the morphology of plant vacuoles correlate with cell size (Owens and Poole, 1979; Berger et al., 1998; Löfke et al., 2013) and, hence, it was tempting to postulate that vacuoles may even drive cellular growth (Marty, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Owens and Poole, 1979; Berger et al., 1998; Löfke et al., 2013).

claim: Plant vacuoles are claimed to be important cellular osmoregulators.
source: Plant vacuoles, inter alia, are claimed to be important cellular osmoregulators, and accordingly, have been hypothesised as contributing to turgor-dependent cellular growth induction (Marty, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Marty, 1999).

claim: Auxin responses have been reported to reduce cellular pressure in cell files facing lateral root primordia.
source: Auxin responses have been reported to reduce cellular pressure in cell files facing lateral root primordia (Peret et al., 2012) and vacuolar morphology alterations have been recently described in endodermal tissues during lateral root emergence (Peret et al., 2012; Vermeer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Peret et al., 2012; Vermeer et al., 2014).

claim: Vacuolar morphology alterations have been recently described in endodermal tissues during lateral root emergence.
source: Auxin responses have been reported to reduce cellular pressure in cell files facing lateral root primordia (Peret et al., 2012) and vacuolar morphology alterations have been recently described in endodermal tissues during lateral root emergence (Peret et al., 2012; Vermeer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Peret et al., 2012; Vermeer et al., 2014).

claim: Auxin could impose a conformational change on the SNARE complex, possibly affecting its stability and activity.
source: Auxin impacts on vacuolar SNAREs in a posttranslational manner and it is tempting to speculate that auxin could impose a conformational change on the SNARE complex, possibly affecting its stability and activity.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism of auxin action on SNAREs.

claim: The auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs could impact on homotypic vacuolar fusion events, leading to smaller luminal structures.
source: Accordingly, the auxin effect on vacuolar SNAREs could impact on homotypic vacuolar fusion events, leading to smaller luminal structures.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism linking SNARE regulation to vacuolar morphology.

claim: A structural role of SNAREs has been envisioned, which could be yet another mechanism to impact on vacuolar organisation.
source: Alternatively, also a structural role of SNAREs has been envisioned (Di Sansebastiano, 2013), which could be yet another mechanism to impact on vacuolar organisation.
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to previous work (Di Sansebastiano, 2013).

claim: Most vacuolar structures are interconnected within an untreated cell.
source: Notably, a recent study suggested that most vacuolar structures are interconnected within an untreated cell (Viotti et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Viotti et al., 2013).

claim: Auxin utilises the plant vacuole as a cellular effector to restrict cellular expansion.
source: We assume that auxin utilises the plant vacuole as a cellular effector to restrict cellular expansion.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental findings.

claim: Previous correlative observations on cell size and vacuolar morphology may not reflect that vacuoles drive growth, but rather rely on a vacuole-dependent cellular mechanism that limits growth.
source: Hence, we conclude that previous correlative observations on cell size and vacuolar morphology (Owens and Poole, 1979; Berger et al., 1998; Löfke et al., 2013) may not reflect that vacuoles drive growth, but rather rely on a vacuole-dependent cellular mechanism that limits growth.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing that auxin uses vacuoles to restrict rather than promote growth.

claim: Auxin coordinates extracellular and intracellular components, such as cell wall acidification and vacuolar morphogenesis, for driving and restricting cellular growth.
source: Our data extends the current view of auxin biology, suggesting that auxin coordinates extracellular and intracellular components, such as cell wall acidification (Sauer and Kleine-Vehn, 2011; Spartz et al., 2014) and vacuolar morphogenesis, for driving and restricting cellular growth.
evidence: Proposed model integrating current findings with previous work on cell wall acidification.

claim: The luminal increase of plant vacuoles alone may not be sufficient to induce larger cell sizes due to cell wall limitations.
source: In this light, the luminal increase of plant vacuoles alone may not be sufficient to induce larger cell sizes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Figure 7—figure supplement 2) due to cell wall limitations.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that increased vacuolar size does not necessarily lead to increased cell size.

claim: Limiting cellular vacuolarisation appears sufficient to restrict cellular growth.
source: In contrast, limiting cellular vacuolarisation appears sufficient to restrict cellular growth.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing that auxin-induced reduction in vacuolar size correlates with growth restriction.

claim: A dual growth mechanism would allow plants to dynamically de- and accelerate cellular expansion, integrating multiple distinct, possibly conflictive internal and external triggers.
source: Such a dual growth mechanism would allow plants to dynamically de- and accelerate cellular expansion, integrating multiple distinct, possibly conflictive internal and external triggers.
evidence: Speculative statement about the broader implications of the proposed dual mechanism.
